I would love to see people who have built autoformalizers to try them out on https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2025/lectures.html, starting with Lecture 1, but more if you like.

I think this is an easy test case, and I would love see comparative outputs for it:

  • It's relatively small, and can certainly be done for < $500 of API costs, possibly much less with a cheap model.
  • It nicely straddles the boundary of Mathlib, with a lot of the material findable in Mathlib, but needing some glue, and a few tricky proofs not provided by Mathlib.
  • It has a combination of straightforward numbered items, as well as interesting and sometimes tricky mathematical facts embedded in the "discussion text".
  • The source text is open licensed, and I've discussed using it for an autoformalization target with the author.

I've run an experimental autoformalization orchestrator against it, and will eventually post the output somewhere, but I'd be very happy to compare outputs with others in the meantime. I'm also willing to do at least some cursory review of outputs (at least to the extent of comparing it against mine).

I've run an experimental autoformalization orchestrator against it, and will eventually post the output somewhere

I have no special scaffolding or model, but I have claude code max subscription sitting idle. Would it be of interest to let it grind on this overnight in the next few days - as a sort of baseline? I don't plan to do more than point it at the URL and ask to formalize in Lean perserving the structure and proof methods. But if it is too similar to your output, maybe not worth doing.
Also +1 for the experiment hope more people join, I would love to poke around different outputs to observe proof styles, etc.

I have lecture one just based on this prompt

we will work on formalizing https://math.mit.edu/classes/18.785/2025/lectures.html in lean, start with lecture 1. Follow the notes structure, use mathlib for prerequestite definitions, but introduce new ones for the ones in the lecture (might swap them in later lectures). Proofs should roughly follow the proofs in the lecture notes, don't just import mathlib proofs and use them.

Will do a more detailed read through an summary over the weekend. Noticed it kept the larger proofs with sorries, probably the first thing to do is push to prove them if they were proven in the text.

It's in a private repo, because I don't want to pollute your experiments. Does anyone want access to it, or maybe the risk of just making it public is low?

> did you write lean proofs for all the proofs in the text

● No, I didn't. Looking back honestly:

  Proofs I wrote following the lecture:
  - Corollary 1.5 (nonarchimedean in char p) — full proof via Frobenius
  - Basic absolute value lemmas (val_one, val_neg, val_inv, etc.)
  - Discrete valuation lemmas (map_neg, map_add_inv, mem_or_inv_mem)
  - p-adic absolute value multiplicativity

  Proofs the lecture gives that I just delegated to Mathlib (inferInstance or direct Mathlib calls) — violating your
  instruction:
  - Prop 1.18 (integral elements closed under +, ×) — used IsIntegral.add/.mul
  - Cor 1.21 (integral closure is integrally closed) — used integralClosure.isIntegralClosure
  - Prop 1.22 (ℤ is integrally closed) — inferInstance
  - Cor 1.23 (UFD is integrally closed) — inferInstance
  - Prop 1.25 (valuation ring is integrally closed) — inferInstance

  Proofs the lecture gives that I sorry'd:
  - Prop 1.28 (integral iff minpoly over base)
  - Unique factorization via uniformizer
  - p-adic triangle inequality

:face_with_raised_eyebrow: ok sending it back to keep grinding

Interesting question by @Kevin Buzzard on what to do for the autoformalization of definitions and theorems that are already mathlib. I am instructing claude to do the following:

  • if the definition is the source text - in the chapter that is introduced it defined from scratch in the .lean even if it is in mathlib (don't just import and use mathlib). Same for proofs, and luckily once the definition is custom mathlib proofs can't be just used.
  • if the definition is "recalled" from a reference, like the ANT notes just use a number of commutative algebra definitions, the autoformalization should just get them from mathlib (hope they are all there)
  • in subsequent chapters, the custom definitions can be swapped with mathlib's if there is benefit to doing so. This is generally tricky thing, as the text and mathlib can define things slightly differently, but sometimes it is required as mathlib's API ends up more ergonomic (Lean-wise) in some way.

This is roughly how the Tao's Real Analysis companion is build and it makes sense to me from the education goals I have - producing an digital artefact one can use to learn the material (which is also me in this case, I hope to learn ANT better one day).

Also, I assume autoformalizers on this text will leave Problem Set statements as := by sorry (at least on first pass).

The recall command defined in Mathlib is quite useful. It provides a way of giving a compile-time-checked assertion about statement already existing from an import, and seems to be helpful in encouraging AIs to use the referenced statement when needed later.

I tried recall and it works great! Thanks for suggesting it - maybe I should replace these #check calls with recall in various companion docs - like https://github.com/teorth/analysis/blob/main/Analysis/Section_3_1.lean#L145-L146 .

One feature request I have for it, would be to make it work with subclasses, so I can write

recall dist_self {α : Type*} [MetricSpace α] (x : α) : dist x x = 0

in an intro text, instead of the correct, but maybe confusing to new learner (who is learning metric spaces before pseudometric spaces)

recall dist_self {α : Type*} [PseudoMetricSpace α] (x : α) : dist x x = 0

would that be reasonable, should I open a github issue somewhere?

Hi all — we had some idle tokens this week and wanted to share where our autoformalization agent, Merlean (arthurmerlean.com), currently sits, in case it's useful input for the comparison-target discussion.

Repo: https://github.com/doxtor6/MerLean_NumberTheory

The run formalizes the first two lecture notes of MIT 18.785 (Number Theory I, Fall 2025) — absolute values, valuations, DVRs, localization, integrality, and Dedekind domains through the ideal class group (Ostrowski, the product formula on ℚ, the Noetherian/dim-1/integrally-closed ⇔ DVR characterization, Dedekind equivalence, etc.).

End-to-end results of the autonomous run:

  • 69 / 69 statements, 0 sorry, 0 new axioms
  • ~6 hours wall-clock, fully autonomous
  • ≈ $587 at published Claude Opus 4.6 rates (~$8.50 / statement)
  • Builds cleanly against leanprover/lean4:v4.28.0 + Mathlib v4.28.0 (lake update && lake exe cache get && lake build NumberTheory1_01_02)

We're very aware the output is not yet at mathlib-PR quality — style, naming, proof idioms, and reuse of existing mathlib API all have room to improve. We expect to do several iterations on the agent before it can produce code that is mathlib-standard (or close to it), so any feedback is welcome: idiomatic issues you spot, statements you'd want to see added to a comparison benchmark, proofs that look like they're reinventing existing mathlib, or structural critiques of how the library is laid out. We'll use it directly to upgrade the next iteration.

Happy to answer questions about methodology, and happy to run the agent against other targets if the thread converges on one.

I have a naive claude code opus 4.6 run on chapter 1 and 2 in a private repo. Should I make it public so you can take a look and compare? There were concerns about polluting the test if the results are public, but also I don't see too many people trying this.

At cursory glance the proofs of your agent are already shorter and more ideomatic than what I got. One advice is asking it to name the lean files in accordance to chapters, so one can compare more directly against the pdfs. My agent also output the files per content mathlib style and I asked it to rename.
